data: © NASA — Apollo 15 mission report. Public domain. Fallen Astronaut sculpture left on the surface.
Descent stage · ALSEP · LRV rover · flag · Fallen Astronaut sculpture

First mission with the Lunar Roving Vehicle — drove 27.9 km. Scott left a small aluminium figurine, 'Fallen Astronaut', and a plaque listing all astronauts and cosmonauts who died in the space race. It is the only artwork on the Moon, left without public announcement at the time.
First crewed surface mobility — extended exploration radius from hundreds of metres to tens of kilometres, the model for crewed Mars surface operations.

Apollo 15 landed in Hadley Rille / Apennine Mountains on July 30, 1971 — the first "J-class" mission with extended surface stay, Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), and a scientist-trained pilot (David Scott). Scott and Irwin drove 28 km total across three EVAs, found the Genesis Rock (~4.1 Ga anorthosite, primary crust), and on live TV dropped a feather + hammer to demonstrate Galileo's gravity test.
Apollo 15 crew + the Lunar Roving Vehicle in pre-mission training — Scott + Irwin would drive the first wheels on the Moon.
Jim Irwin saluting beside the LRV with Mt Hadley Delta behind — the first images of the Apennine Mountains from the surface.
David Scott at the rim of Hadley Rille — first time astronauts stood at the edge of an ancient lava channel on another world.
Hadley Plain panorama — Falcon descent stage + LRV + Mt Hadley Delta on the horizon.
Sample 15415 "Genesis Rock" — pure ferroan anorthosite, ~4.1 billion years old. A fragment of the Moon's primary magma-ocean crust.
Orrery reference map of LROC imagery and the Apollo 15 traverse data

Illustrated block map of the Apollo 15 landing site beside Hadley Rille: in the centre are the Falcon lunar module, the ALSEP science station and the Lunar Rover; traverse routes lead to Station 1 (Elbow), Station 2 (St. George), Station 4 (Dune) and Station 7 (Spur).
